## Question 1: Warm-up

Before mapping anything, get oriented in the data.

a)  Using `tabyl()`, show the breakdown of `reason` (reason for discharge). Which reason is most common, and what percentage of all discharges does it account for?

b)  Make one bar chart showing the number of discharges by `services_d` (type of treatment service). Give it an informative title and axis labels.

c)  In a sentence or two: what does the `reason` value "Transferred to another treatment program or facility" mean for our completion percentages? If a state transfers a lot of patients, would its completion rate look higher or lower than a state that transfers very few?

> **Full credit:** a working `tabyl()`, a readable labeled bar chart, and a sentence or two showing you thought about part (c). There is no trick in this question!

```{r}
#| label: q1.1 ANSWER

### Using tabyl(), show the breakdown of reason (reason for discharge). Which reason is most common, and what percentage of all discharges does it account for?
class(teds_d$reason)
#look at this variable; check class
summary(teds_d$reason)
#summary of data frame

teds_d <- teds_d %>%
  mutate(reason = recode(as.character(reason),
                         "1" = "Treatment completed",
                         "2" = "Dropped out of treatment",
                         "3" = "Terminated by facility",
                         "4" = "Transferred to another treatment program or facility",
                         "5" = "Incarcerated",
                         "6" = "Death",
                         "7" = "Other",
                         .missing = "unknown"),
         reason = factor(reason))
# ////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
# "Turn the codes into text, swap each code for its label (and call missing ones 'unknown'),
# then treat the result as a category (factor)."

#######checkin data
teds_d %>% 
  tabyl(reason) %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%  # arranges in descending order
  adorn_pct_formatting(digit = 2) # rounds to 2 decimal digits
```

The reason for discharge that was the most common was due to treatment being completed, which occurred 47.80% of the time.

**Answer to (a): refer to label: "q1.1 ANSWER"**

**Answer to (b):** (produce a bar chart in the code chunk above) **refer to label: "q1.2 ANSWER"**

**Answer to (c):** "Transferred to another treatment program or facility" may or may not mean something for the completion percentages, depending on how the "Transferred to (...)" designation is handled.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| **is treatment complete** | **record updated locally** | **result** |
| Y | Y | increase in local completion |
| Y | N | no change in local, recorded still as transferred |
| N | Y | no change in local, recorded still as transferred |
| N | N | no change in local, recorded still as transferred |

**If a state transfers a lot of patients, would its completion rate look higher or lower than a state that transfers very few?**

For a state with many transfer patients, the completion rate (%) would look higher when the majority of patients that transferred have not completed treatment, and lower when the majority of patients that transferred actually completed treatment.

## Question 2: Mapping no use at discharge

Make **one [*interactive*]{.underline} map** with `ggiraph` showing, for each state, the percentage of [completed treatment]{.underline} episodes that ended with [no use at discharge]{.underline}.

In other words: among the episodes where `reason` is "Treatment completed," what share had `freq1_d` equal to "no use"?

Work through this in bite-sized steps, like we did in Part 2. You will need to filter, group, summarize, build an index, join, and plot. Write one step at a time and look at the result before moving on.

```{r}
#| label: percentage per state
#grouping the treatment completed cleaned dataset by state

percent_completed_by_state <- filtered_my_teds_d |> #takes teds dataset, each row is a specific record (left for a various reason)
  group_by(stfips) |> # group by stfips code

            no_use_cases = sum(freq1_d == "no use", na.rm = TRUE)) |>  # na.rm removes na values if they exist
  mutate(percentage_completed = (no_use_cases / total_cases) * 100)

percent_completed_by_state
```

```{r}
#| label: WORKS; checking individual state for count "no use"
```

DENOMINATOR I USED: I chose to not include the "unknown" values of freq1_d as that is what is considered as the best practice to follow when dealing with the subject matter of standard public health reporting and data analytics.\
Including uncertain (in this case, unknown) data in the total count would artificially deflate the calculated percentage, which would be a misrepresentation of the accurately recorded data.

### The denominator decision

About a third of the `freq1_d` values in this dataset are "unknown." That means you have to decide what your denominator is, and there is more than one defensible answer:

- **All** completed episodes, counting "unknown" in the denominator, or

- Only completed episodes where frequency of use was **actually recorded**.

Pick one. **Below your map, write one sentence saying which denominator you used and why.** Either choice can earn full credit. Missing description earns no points for this portion.

### Your map must:

- be interactive (rendered with `girafe()`)

- show a tooltip with the state name and the percentage, rounded to two decimal places

- have a title and a legend label that say what is being shown

- handle states with no data honestly (remember Friday in class)

> **Full credit:** one interactive map meeting the four requirements above, plus your denominator sentence. It does not have to be beautiful, only correct and readable.

## Question 3: Service type and length of stay

Treatment outcomes can vary depending on the type of service a patient receives and how long they stay in treatment.

Investigate how **completion rates** differ across **service type** (`services_d`) and **length of stay** (`los`).

- Create **two** visualizations: at least one focused on service type, and at least one focused on length of stay. These do not need to be maps, and they do not need to be interactive. Pick whatever chart type makes the pattern easiest to see.

- Then write a short summary (3-ish sentences, full grammatical sentences) explaining the main patterns you observe.

**One warning:** look up `los` in the codebook *before* you calculate anything with it. Code that runs without an error can still give you a meaningless answer.

> **Full credit:** two labeled visualizations that actually show the comparison you say they show, plus a summary that describes a real pattern in your own output. You are not graded on finding the "right" pattern. You are graded on whether your summary matches your charts.

```{r}
# 2. Use group_by(services_d) instead of group_by(stfips).
# 3. In summarize(), count all rows with n() and completed rows with sum(reason == "Treatment completed").
# 4. Use mutate() to calculate the percentage, the same as in Q2.

percent_of_completion_by_services_d <- my_teds_d_services_d_fresh |>
  group_by(services_d) |> # group by services_d
  summarize(total_cases_services_d = n(), # n() is to count rows/TOTAL ROWS
            treatment_completed_cases_services_d = sum(reason == "Treatment completed", na.rm = TRUE)) |>  # na.rm removes na values if they exist
  mutate(percentage_completed_services_d = (treatment_completed_cases_services_d / total_cases_services_d) * 100)

summary(percent_of_completion_by_services_d)
percent_of_completion_by_services_d
```

```{r}
#| label: q3.1 ANSWER

plot_percent_of_completion_by_services_d <- ggplot(data = percent_of_completion_by_services_d,

      text = paste(
        "Type of treatment service/setting at discharge:", services_d,
        "<br>Percentage completed:", round(percentage_completed_services_d, 2), "%"))) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() + # flips cooordinates; can use y = within aes() instead too
  labs(title = "Percent of Completed Treatment Discharges by Type of treatment service/setting at discharge, 2024 TEDS-D",
       y = "% of discharges",
       x = "Type of treatment service/setting at discharge") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + #doesn't shift title to center??
  theme_minimal()
ggplotly(plot_percent_of_completion_by_services_d, tooltip = "text")
```

```{r}
# make a grouped version of los with case_when() inside mutate().
my_teds_d_los <- my_teds_d_los %>%
  mutate(
    binned_los = case_when(
      los >= 1 & los <= 7 ~ "1 ~ 7 days",
      los >= 8 & los <= 14 ~ "8 ~ 14 days",
      los >= 15 & los <= 30 ~ "15 ~ 30 days",
      los == 31 ~ "31 to 45 days",
      los == 32 ~ "46 to 60 days",
      los == 33 ~ "61 to 90 days",
      los == 34 ~ "91 to 120 days",
      los == 35 ~ "121 to 180 days",
      los == 36 ~ "181 to 365 days",
      los == 37 ~ "Over 365 days"
    )
  )

####CHECKING DATA AGAIN
my_teds_d_los %>% 
  tabyl(los) %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%  # arranges in descending order
  adorn_totals("row") %>% # shows total of variables being checked
  adorn_pct_formatting(digit = 2) # rounds to 2 decimal digits
```

```{r}
# 2. Use group_by(services_d) instead of group_by(stfips).
# 3. In summarize(), count all rows with n() and completed rows with sum(reason == "Treatment completed").
# 4. Use mutate() to calculate the percentage, the same as in Q2.

percent_by_binned_los <- my_teds_d_los |>
  group_by(binned_los) |> # group by binned los
  summarize(total_cases_los = n(), # n() is to count rows/TOTAL ROWS
            treatment_completed_cases_los = sum(reason == "Treatment completed", na.rm = TRUE)) |>  # na.rm removes na values if they exist
  mutate(percentage_completed_los = (treatment_completed_cases_los / total_cases_los) * 100)

summary(percent_by_binned_los)
percent_by_binned_los
```
